title: Joshua 16:5–10
context: The narrator now gives Ephraim's specific territory within Joseph's lot, tracing its borders from the Jordan to the sea and noting towns set apart for Ephraim inside Manasseh's land. The chapter ends, like chapter 15, with an honest report of incomplete obedience: the Canaanites of Gezer were not driven out but put to forced labor.

verses.text: This was the border of the children of Ephraim according to their families. The border of their inheritance eastward was Ataroth Addar, to Beth Horon the upper.
verses.arminianNotes: Ephraim, the younger son, is described first. Arminian readers note that Jacob had placed Ephraim ahead of Manasseh (Genesis 48:19), and they see Ephraim called to live up to that blessing in faithful conduct.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jacob said "his younger brother will be greater than he" (Genesis 48:19). God's choice of the younger over the older, a recurring biblical pattern, shapes even the order of the allotment.

verses.text: The border went out westward at Michmethath on the north. The border turned about eastward to Taanath Shiloh, and passed along it on the east of Janoah.
verses.arminianNotes: Michmethath and Taanath Shiloh mark the northern turns of the line. Arminian readers note that clear borders protected peace between tribes, and keeping them was part of Israel's shared covenant responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God's ordering in defined boundaries. The same God who sets bounds for the nations (compare Deuteronomy 32:8) sets them for the tribes, giving each its place within his people.

verses.text: It went down from Janoah to Ataroth, to Naarah, reached to Jericho, and went out at the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes: The eastern border descends through Ataroth and Naarah to Jericho and the Jordan. Arminian readers note that Jericho, where Israel's conquest began by faith (Joshua 6), now marks the edge of Ephraim's settled inheritance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a fitting reminder in Jericho's appearance here. The first city God gave Israel by his own hand now borders Ephraim's land, so the inheritance is framed by a memorial of God's power.

verses.text: From Tappuah the border went along westward to the brook of Kanah; and ended at the sea. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Ephraim according to their families;
verses.arminianNotes: The western line follows "the brook of Kanah" to the sea, and the summary names Ephraim's inheritance. Arminian readers see a complete gift that Ephraim is now responsible to hold faithfully for future generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the formula "This is the inheritance of the tribe" as the record of God's settled allotment. Ephraim later becomes a leading northern tribe, and its place in Israel's story starts with this gift.

verses.text: together with the cities which were set apart for the children of Ephraim in the middle of the inheritance of the children of Manasseh, all the cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Some cities were "set apart for the children of Ephraim in the middle of the inheritance of the children of Manasseh." Arminian readers see brother tribes called to share land and live together in cooperation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's distribution is not rigid but provides for the needs of each tribe. Joseph's two tribes are bound together, their territories interwoven by God's arrangement.

verses.text: They didn’t drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer; but the Canaanites dwell in the territory of Ephraim to this day, and have become servants to do forced labor.
verses.arminianNotes: Ephraim "didn't drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer" but made them forced laborers (compare Judges 1:29; Joshua 17:13). Arminian readers see a choice of profit over full obedience, with lasting consequences for Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see real failure here, noting that compromise with the Canaanites later became a snare (Judges 2:20–22). They add that God remained faithful, and Gezer came fully under Israel in Solomon's day (1 Kings 9:16).
